source: Fikes and Nilsson (1971) STRIPS: a new approach to the application of theorem proving to problem solving
finding: STRIPS describes each action by a precondition list, a delete list and an add list over a world model of logic formulas. The planner searches by means-ends analysis: pick a difference between the state and the goal, choose an action whose add list removes it, and make that action's preconditions the new subgoal. Built for the Shakey robot.
numbers: Not opened this session (PDF fetch failed). No benchmark numbers from memory.
limits: From memory [M]. The original also used a resolution theorem prover to test preconditions. Later work (Lifschitz 1986) gave STRIPS a clean semantics.
agent_relevance: This is the root of O5 work backwards: goal minus add list plus preconditions is the regression step. Each action needs explicit preconditions and effects.

source: Bylander (1994) The computational complexity of propositional STRIPS planning
finding: Deciding whether a propositional STRIPS problem has a plan is PSPACE-complete in general. Several restricted classes are NP-complete or polynomial. Finding a shortest plan is harder than finding any plan.
numbers: No numbers; complexity classes only (from memory).
limits: From memory [M]; exact restricted classes not re-checked. Worst case only: real benchmark domains are far easier.
agent_relevance: Planning without a bound is worst-case hard, so the scaffold must keep a step budget and treat success of backward search as a bonus, not a guarantee.

source: McDermott et al. (1998) PDDL: the Planning Domain Definition Language
finding: PDDL was written for the AIPS-98 competition as one shared syntax: typed objects, predicates, actions with :precondition and :effect, and an optional ADL fragment (quantifiers, conditional effects).
numbers: Not opened (fetch returned a non-PDF). The adoption fact is confirmed in the IPC-3 paper (see a07).
limits: From memory [M]. The syntax is lisp-like and deliberately close to STRIPS.
agent_relevance: PDDL is a ready-made, checkable format for an action model. A schema slot can ask the model to write an action as name, preconditions, effects.

source: Blum and Furst (1997) Fast planning through planning graph analysis; Kautz and Selman SATPLAN
finding: Graphplan builds a layered graph of facts and actions with mutual-exclusion links, then searches it backward from the goals. It was far faster than older partial-order planners and led to SAT-based planning.
numbers: No numbers retained (from memory).
limits: From memory [M]. Graphplan-style and SAT planners dominated the early competitions and were then overtaken by heuristic forward search (confirmed for 2000 in a07).
agent_relevance: Backward search is cheap only after a forward reachability check prunes impossible subgoals; a cheap forward feasibility pass before O5 is a candidate design.

source: Bonet and Geffner (2001) Planning as heuristic search (HSP)
finding: HSP derives a heuristic automatically from the STRIPS description by solving a relaxed problem that ignores delete lists, then runs forward search with it. The same method works on any domain with no hand-tuned heuristic.
numbers: No numbers retained (from memory).
limits: From memory [M]. The h_add estimate is not admissible, so it finds plans but not always short plans.
agent_relevance: The relaxation idea: drop the side effects, count the steps to each goal fact. A cheap relaxed estimate of subgoal difficulty could rank candidate subgoals at S6.

source: Hoffmann and Nebel (2001) The FF planning system: fast plan generation through heuristic search
finding: FF takes the relaxed-plan length (delete effects ignored) as heuristic, uses enforced hill-climbing, and prunes with helpful actions. It won the automated track of the 2000 competition.
numbers: The fetched file was unreadable (font encoding), so no numbers were extracted. The IPC-3 paper (a07) confirms FF as a top fully automated planner in 2002.
limits: Opened:false because the text could not be read. Relaxed-plan heuristics fail on domains with dead ends or resource limits.
agent_relevance: Shows that search guided by a goal-distance estimate beat blind search by large factors; supports pairing O5 with an estimate rather than raw backchaining.

source: Long and Fox (2003) The 3rd International Planning Competition: results and analysis
finding: Describes the competition series. 1998: 5 STRIPS planners, McDermott organised, PDDL adopted as the shared language, hand-coded control allowed but nobody used it. 2000: 17 planners, split into hand-coded and fully automated, forward heuristic search was the best automated approach. 2002: temporal and numeric tracks.
numbers: 2002 event: 26 domains, 20 instances each, nearly 1000 instances, about half meant for fully automated planners. A one-number scoring function in 1998 gave counter-intuitive results and was dropped for two measures: plan length and time.
quote: it is impossible to make unequivocal decisions about which system is best
limits: Data were collected during the contest, with no later controlled experiments, so cross-domain conclusions are weak. The authors say so.
agent_relevance: Even with five planners no single best system could be named. For our agent: report plan length and cost separately, not one score.

source: Long and Fox (2003) 3rd IPC: hand-coded control knowledge
finding: In 2002 the hand-coded planners (TLPlan, TALPlanner, SHOP2) produced plans of high quality with dramatic speed. TLPlan got a prize for best performance. SHOP2 attempted every problem type and solved almost all. Hand-written rules beat domain-independent search, but the effort to write them could not be measured.
numbers: Table lists TLPlan 610 problems at 100% and TALPlanner 50 and 102 at 100%; SHOP2 listed at 99% with 331 and 508 in one row (column meaning not fully clear from the text layout).
quote: we failed to find any way to usefully quantify this effort
limits: Effort to write the rules was not quantified: the authors say they failed to find a way. Hand-coded planners were also given large extra instances.
agent_relevance: Domain knowledge written by a person is the strongest planner input. For us: a good action model per task type is worth more than a clever generic search.

source: Fox and Long (2003) PDDL2.1: an extension to PDDL for expressing temporal planning domains
finding: PDDL2.1 adds numeric fluents and durative actions in five levels: level 1 is plain STRIPS, level 2 numeric, level 3 discretised durative actions, level 4 continuous durative actions, level 5 events and processes. It also defines formal semantics and validation of concurrent plans.
numbers: 5 expressiveness levels; level 4 was not used in the 2002 competition. The authors say the language exceeds the power of current planners.
limits: Language-level paper: no performance numbers.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean ladder from simple precondition-effect actions to time and resources; the scaffold needs only level 1 plus a numeric budget.

source: Helmert (2006) The Fast Downward planning system
finding: Fast Downward translates PDDL to a multi-valued state representation and uses a causal-graph heuristic with hierarchical decomposition. It became the standard open-source planner and the base for later LLM planning work.
numbers: No numbers retained; not opened (download failed).
limits: From memory [M]. Later papers in this file use it as the ground-truth solver (a14, a17, a18).
agent_relevance: The standard external solver for LLM-plus-planner hybrids, so an LLM-built model can be checked or solved by it.

source: Valmeekam, Olmo, Sreedharan, Kambhampati (2022) PlanBench
finding: A benchmark of IPC-style domains (Blocksworld, Logistics and obfuscated variants) with several tasks: plan generation, optimal planning, verification, execution reasoning, replanning, generalisation. LLMs fall well short on plan generation.
numbers: GPT-4 solved 206/600 (34.3%) of Blocksworld plan generation, Instruct-GPT3 41/600 (6.8%).
limits: Task-level rows in the extracted table were misaligned, so only plan generation is quoted. Blocksworld of 3-5 blocks is small.
agent_relevance: Baseline for why a planning scaffold must not rely on a bare model writing a whole plan.

source: Valmeekam, Sreedharan, Marquez, Olmo, Kambhampati (2023) On the planning abilities of LLMs: a critical investigation
finding: Autonomous mode: GPT-3, Instruct-GPT3 and BLOOM almost never produce an executable goal-reaching plan. Humans did far better.
numbers: Plan generation 6/600 (1%) GPT-3, 41/600 (6.8%) Instruct-GPT3, 4/250 (1.6%) BLOOM; optimal planning 0.3%, 5.8%, 2%; replanning 7.8%, 6.6%, 3%. Human baseline 78% valid (39 of 50) and 89.7% of those optimal (35). Average over benchmark about 3%.
limits: Small Blocksworld (up to 5 blocks, optimal length mostly 8). Old models. Human baseline is preliminary.
agent_relevance: Plan generation from the model alone is the weak step; checking and repair with an outside tool is where value was found.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) On the planning abilities: heuristic and human-in-the-loop modes
finding: Using the LLM plan as the starting plan for the LPG planner helped somewhat. In a user study, planners helped by LLM suggestions were somewhat more accurate but the gain was small.
numbers: LPG-seeded runs: average LLM plan length 7.22 and final plan length 11.7 on the 600 instances. Human study: 17 of 23 (74%) correct in one group, 18 of 22 (82%) in the LLM-hint group.
limits: The gain is small and not tested for significance; 45 participants in this arm.
agent_relevance: LLM output works as a rough seed that an exact tool completes, not as a final plan.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) PlanBench: disguised domains and goal shuffling
finding: Renaming actions and predicates (Mystery Blocksworld) and shuffling goal order breaks the models. Success on Blocksworld looks like pattern matching to training text, not planning.
numbers: Mystery Blocksworld plan generation: GPT-3 0/600, Instruct-GPT3 7/600 (1.1%), BLOOM 0/50. Goal-shuffle robustness: GPT-3 20.3%, Instruct-GPT3 60.5%, BLOOM 5%. Plan generalisation (loops): 0%, 17%, 0%.
limits: Instruct-GPT3 was the best model; stronger models later score higher (see a16).
agent_relevance: Do not trust a plan format that depends on familiar names. The scaffold can rename or abstract surface words as a test of whether the plan still holds (a form of G3).

source: Valmeekam, Stechly, Kambhampati (2024) LLMs still cannot plan; can large reasoning models? (o1 on PlanBench)
finding: o1-preview and o1-mini beat all earlier LLMs on PlanBench but are not robust: performance falls with plan length and with obfuscation. Fast Downward still solves everything in a fraction of a second.
numbers: Blocksworld zero-shot: o1-preview 587/600 (97.8%), o1-mini 340/600 (56.6%), Fast Downward 600/600 in 0.265 s versus 40.43 s for o1-preview. Mystery Blocksworld: 52.8% o1-preview, 19.1% o1-mini. Randomized Mystery: 37.3% (one-shot 41.6%). Best earlier LLM on plain Blocksworld: LLaMA 3.1 405B at 62.6%. Longer plans (20-40 steps, 110 instances): 23.63%.
quote: LLMs struggle on even the smallest instances
limits: Preview versions with capped reasoning tokens. Reported cost about $1,897 for the o1 experiments.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models close much of the gap on short plans but pay seconds and dollars for what a solver does instantly; supports calling a solver tool for narrow formal cases.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2024) o1 on unsolvable instances
finding: On 100 unsolvable problems, o1-preview correctly said impossible only a minority of the time and often returned a made-up plan. It also wrongly declared some solvable problems impossible.
numbers: Blocksworld: 27% correctly identified unsolvable, 19% empty plan, 54% a full but wrong plan. Randomized Mystery: 16% correct, 5% empty plan, 79% full wrong plan. 11.5% of 600 solvable Mystery instances wrongly called impossible (0% on plain Blocksworld).
limits: Only one model family tested; 100 unsolvable instances.
agent_relevance: Backward search that never reaches the initial state is evidence of impossibility; the schema should allow a no-plan-found result (note the tension with G6, which forbids abstaining on the first pass).

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLMs can't plan, but can help planning in LLM-Modulo frameworks
finding: Position paper: the LLM generates candidate plans, external critics (VAL and other model-based checkers) verify, and a back-prompt loop repairs. Autonomous LLM planning is approximate retrieval; guarantees come only from the sound verifier.
numbers: Cites earlier results: with VAL back-prompting up to 15 rounds, Blocksworld reached 82% and Logistics 70%; obfuscated Mystery Blocksworld only about 10%. Best plain-LLM strategies on the obfuscated set reached about 0.7%.
limits: Numbers are quoted from the authors' own earlier paper (not independent). Position paper, not a new experiment.
agent_relevance: Matches our G2 and G5: code or tool verifies, the model proposes; shows where it still fails (when the model cannot make plausible candidates).

source: Liu et al. (2023) LLM+P: empowering LLMs with optimal planning proficiency
finding: GPT-4 writes a PDDL problem file from natural language, Fast Downward solves it, GPT-4 translates the plan back. Much better than asking GPT-4 for the plan directly; a Tree-of-Thought style search was also poor. Needs a human-written domain file.
numbers: Temperature 0, 200 s planner limit, 20 tasks per domain, 7 IPC domains. Table text is jumbled, but LLM+P reaches about 90% on Blocksworld and about 85-95% on some other domains; direct LLM as planner scored 0-35% and the ToT variant 0-10% in most domains; some domains (for example Floortile) were 0 for all.
limits: Columns could not be assigned exactly from the PDF layout; the ranges above are approximate. Domain PDDL is given by a person, so the hard modelling step is not tested.
agent_relevance: Shows the value of moving the model's job from planning to translating into a formal action model that a solver can use.

source: Silver et al. (2023) Generalized planning in PDDL domains with pretrained LLMs
finding: GPT-4 is asked to write a Python program (no search) that solves all tasks in a PDDL domain, from a few training tasks, with automated debugging against the training tasks (up to 4 repair rounds) and optional chain-of-thought summary. It matched or beat generalised-planning baselines in several domains.
numbers: 7 domains, 10 seeds, 30 evaluation tasks per seed. GPT-4 fraction solved: Delivery 0.90, Forest 1.00, Gripper 0.90, Ferry 0.80, Heavy 0.60, Spanner 0.10, Miconic 0.01 (as extracted). Without debugging: Delivery 0.10, Forest 0.62, Gripper 0.50. Without PDDL names: about 0.10 in most. GPT-3.5 mostly 0.00. Error types over training tasks: Python exception 40.0%, plan semantics 34.0%, plan syntax 13.0%, timeout 13.0%.
limits: Domain names carry meaning, and removing them drops results sharply. Evaluation on larger tasks than training. The Ferry/Spanner/Heavy/Miconic row mapping is from a partly misaligned table.
agent_relevance: Strongest case that a model can write the rule of the plan (a program) and a checker finds the faults. Debugging against larger tasks mirrors G3.

source: Guan et al. (2023) Leveraging pretrained LLMs to construct and utilize world models for model-based task planning
finding: GPT-4 builds the PDDL action model (preconditions and effects) in natural-language dialogue with PDDL validators and humans; Fast Downward then plans. Correcting the model once is cheaper than correcting each plan.
numbers: Over 40 actions and 400+ literals in total (41 actions); 27 Household and 21 Logistics tasks. Fast Downward with the corrected LLM model: 95% Household, 100% Logistics. Only-LLM planner: 15% and 0%. ReAct about 33% Household; LLM plus VAL back-prompt with LLM-built model about 48% Household (cells partly misaligned in extraction).
limits: Human feedback used to fix the model. Few domains; GPT-4 sometimes fails to use feedback.
agent_relevance: Directly supports giving the agent an explicit action model (precondition, effect) and solving over it instead of free-form chain of thought.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the self-verification limitations of LLMs on reasoning and planning tasks
finding: GPT-4 critiquing its own plans did not help and in other domains hurt; a sound external verifier raised accuracy. Re-prompting with only a yes/no from a sound verifier kept most of the gain.
numbers: 100 instances per domain. Blocksworld: standard prompting 40%, LLM+LLM binary feedback 55%, LLM+sound verifier 60% (binary), 87% (first-error), 83% (all-error); sampling k=15 68%, k=25 72%; self-consistency 42%. Mystery Blocksworld: 4%, 0%, 10%, 8%, 6%, 9%, 14%, 4%. Game of 24: 5% to 36-38% with sound verifier.
limits: Columns were reassembled from a flattened table; column order assumed. Only GPT-4 and three domains.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2 and G5: the model is a weak verifier of its own plans; use a state-simulating check.

source: Katz, Kokel, Srinivas, Sohrabi (2024) Thought of Search: planning with language models through the lens of efficiency
finding: Instead of calling the LLM at every search step, ask it once for the successor function and goal test as code, then run ordinary BFS or DFS. This keeps soundness and completeness and needs few LLM calls.
numbers: BlocksWorld: all 502 tasks solved by all 5 generated pairs (100%), total time 0.56 s to 9.7 s; correct code after 2.8 iterations for the successor function and 1 for the goal test on average. 1362 Game of 24 instances at 100%. 4000 PrOntoQA questions at 100%.
limits: Blocks are small (4-5 blocks). Wrong code makes wrong search; hand-set unit tests needed.
agent_relevance: The most direct design lesson: use the model to write the action model once, run the search in plain code. This is the program-does-the-control split in our SCHEMA section 1.

source: Xie et al. (2023) Translating natural language to planning goals with large language models
finding: GPT-3.5 translates English goals to PDDL goals well for plain cases and fills in missing details from commonsense, but fails with numbers or spatial reasoning and is sensitive to the prompt.
numbers: Blocksworld goal translation at 8 blocks: roughly 67-75% for some tasks and near 100% for others; some ALFRED subtasks about 50-60%. Direct planning success near 0% for most tasks.
limits: Percentages read from a partly garbled table, so ranges are not exact. GPT-3.5 variants only.
agent_relevance: Goal translation is the safer LLM job; spatial and numeric goals need a code check.

source: Oswald, Srinivas, Kokel, Lee, Katz, Sohrabi (2024) Large language models as planning domain generators
finding: Tests 7 LLMs on writing PDDL domains from text across 9 domains and 3 description classes, scored by comparing the top-100 plans from the generated domain with the true domain. Moderate skill, grows with model size.
numbers: Best model (LLaMA-2-70b) produced valid PDDL in 94% of domains and heuristically equivalent domains in 25%. Flipped description class boosted results by about 10%. Evaluation used K planner and VAL.
limits: Equivalence is judged by plan overlap on 2 simple problems per domain, so false matches are possible. Older open models.
agent_relevance: Writing a full action model is still error prone without feedback; keep validators in the loop.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Natural Plan: benchmarking LLMs on natural language planning
finding: A planning test in natural language (trip, meetings, calendar) with tool outputs given as context. Solve rate falls with problem size and does not improve much with self-correction or long context.
numbers: Trip Planning exact match: GPT-3.5 7.3%, GPT-4 31.1%, GPT-4o 3.7%, Gemini 1.5 Flash 25.6%, Gemini 1.5 Pro 34.8%. Meeting: 19.1%, 47.0%, 45.2%, 23.9%, 39.1%. Calendar: 19.9%, 41.2%, 43.7%, 34.3%, 48.9%. All models below 5% with 10 cities.
limits: Constraint-satisfaction style rather than action-effect planning. Cell order assumed from the header.
agent_relevance: Shows planning breaks as the number of interacting constraints grows; supports a step budget and decomposition.

source: Pallagani et al. (2023) Understanding the capabilities of LLMs for automated planning
finding: Evaluates several LLMs on planning across IPC domains and finds that fine-tuned smaller models can reach good validity inside their training domains but do not carry over to new ones.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers retained.
limits: From memory [M]; arXiv id not verified this session.
agent_relevance: Domain-specific tuning does not transfer; a case for a general scaffold rather than tuned plans.

source: Haslum, Lipovetzky, Magazzeni, Muise (2019) An introduction to the planning domain definition language
finding: Book-length treatment of PDDL: types, predicates, action schemas with preconditions and effects, derived predicates, conditional effects, and how domain models are written and debugged. Complements Ghallab, Nau, Traverso (2004) Automated Planning: Theory and Practice.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: From memory [M].
agent_relevance: Practical guide for writing the action-model slot of the schema.

source: Lifschitz (1986) On the semantics of STRIPS
finding: Gave STRIPS a state-transition semantics: the result of an action is the state minus the delete list plus the add list. This fixed ambiguity about what a STRIPS operator means.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: From memory [M].
agent_relevance: Useful for a verifier: simulate state = (state minus delete) plus add, and check preconditions, in plain code.
